mass.inertiaSource: Ixx/Iyy/Izz/Ixz kg.m2 about the CG. DERIVED 2026-11-02, docs/aircraft/extra-300-inertia-DERIVATION.md: a part-by-part build-up (engine from FAA TCDS 1E4 Note 5, propeller, occupants, fuel, structure) solved against the certificated CG, replacing 800/1100/1800/30 which had no derivation behind them. The PITCH inertia nearly doubles (1100 -> 2038, ky 1.16 -> 1.58 m): the old number was a light-aircraft rule of thumb for an aeroplane whose payload sits near the CG, which an Extra's does not. Izz - Ixx, which is what the inertial couple (Izz-Ixx).p.r uses to hold a spin flat, goes from 1000 to 1874 - Ty 2026-11-09, flying it: the Extra "is too stable... it doesn't spin flat enough and can't tumble".

surfaces._airfoilNote: Ty 2026-11-10, told 26 of the 32 types fly their fin on a 2-D section: "All 26, own build". naca0012-like is 6.30/rad and NOTHING on this path applies a finite-span correction - a vStab never goes through FiniteSpanSection - so these fins carried about 69 % too much directional stiffness at small sideslip. fin-lowAR is 3.724/rad, no camber, zero Cm, Cl_max 1.16 held flat from 25 to 30 deg: a low-aspect-ratio plate, which is what a fin is, and what the rudder on this same tail already used. The hStab is deliberately NOT touched - that is the flat-plate fabric-tail question and it is separate.

crossflow._camberNote: Sideslip -> nose down (owner Ty, 2026-11-01): low pressure over the turtledeck against higher pressure under the fuselage lifts the aft body, and low pressure under the cowling against higher pressure above pulls the nose down -- both even in beta, so either direction pitches down. The turtledeck half was already authored; cowlCamberCl was 0.0 and AeroModel gates on > 0.0, so the forward half never acted. 0.6 against the turtledeck's 1.0: a cowl's flat-top/round-belly section is the shallower of the two. At 50 m/s and 20 deg of sideslip the cowl adds about -196 N.m to the turtledeck's -942.

spinAero.controlSpoilerKSource: A deflected control on a BROADSIDE surface acts as a spoiler on the separated wake, not as a flap: k*sin(delta)*|sin(alpha_chord)|*q*S normal to the FIXED surface, on hinged tail strips, ramped in over 30-50 deg of the strip's own flow angle. SAME VALUE AND SAME MECHANISM AS THE PITTS, which Ty flew and confirmed on 2026-11-10 ("That is it! Now it behaves like a Pitts really does"), applied here on his "The extra was lacking both rudder and elevator power at high alpha". MEASURED: the Extra was worse off than the Pitts had been - elevator 1.9/1.7/0.1 deg/s2 at alpha 90/80/70 and rudder 0.0/1.0/1.4, at the spin's own rates (SpinAuthorityProbe, SPIN_AUTH=1 SPIN_AUTH_ID=extra-300-like). At 0.6: elevator 15.0/14.5/12.1 and rudder 5.7/6.7/4.8, with the spin itself unchanged (226 deg/s at 50 kt against 220 at 50). FINSIDEWASHK IS DELIBERATELY NOT SET HERE, and it was measured first: the Extra's fin stands too far off a body with no measured stations for the crossflow amplification to reach, so 0.5 bought its rudder only 1.0 -> 1.4 deg/s2 at alpha 80 while slowing the spin 220 -> 196 deg/s, and 0.7 stopped it spinning at all (102 kt). The Pitts needed both because its fin sits low against a deep fuselage; this one needs only the spoiler. DOES NOT CHANGE THE ENDO: measured across ExtraEndoProbe's six entries at k 0, 0.6 and 1.0, every one is identical to the turn - the endo runs at alpha -8..41, below where this ramps in, and it was already turning 1.9-2.0 pitch turns at a sustained 113 deg/s.
spinAero.shadowKSource: Geometric helical shadow depth (TailWake.GeometricShadow): the share of dynamic pressure a fully shadowed strip loses. Replaces the Report 648 wake correlation for EVERY surface of this type, and brings in the fuselage's own shadow on the tail and the wings (TailWake.BodyStation). Ty 2026-11-08: "expand the shadow work to all 6 shipping aircraft include the shadow effects of the fuselage on the tail and wing's too". 0.5 is the depth fitted on the Pitts against the owner's spin attitudes on 2026-11-08, and it is a PHYSICAL statement - half the q is gone where a wake fully covers a section - rather than a per-type fudge, so the six carry the same number until a type's own evidence moves it. What differs between types is the geometry, which is the point: the Pitts' cellule shadows itself, the Extra's stabiliser spans well outside its fuselage and is barely shadowed at all (measured in a tumble: tail q 1.00 -> 0.96), and the fuselage's own shadow is what takes the fin in an upright flat spin while leaving it in clear air inverted.

propulsion.dryBoundaryExcessSource: Dry boundary friction excess at rest, over the power curve's own running friction intercept (PistonEngine.BoundaryFrictionFactor): 4.09 means this engine resists 5.09x its running friction when it is dead and dry. Lycoming AEIO-540, 540 cu in, 6 cyl, CR 8.7. SOLVED 2026-11-10 (lane/claude-boundary-friction, CompressionStopProbe with COMPSTOP=1 SOLVE=1) against Ty's anchor "Cranking resistance should be calibrated such that at fine pitch the prop stops right at level flight stall speed", and then his "fix it per engine": it is the one value that puts the measured stopping speed on this type's OWN stall speed, 28.5 m/s = 64 mph (PracticeScenario.EstimateVso, sea level, flaps up - the number the rest of the suite is tuned against, not a book figure). Solved and not predicted: nothing inside an engine explains the fleet's spread, because motoring friction and rated torque both scale with displacement - see PistonEngine.BoundaryExcessFor for what was tried and rejected. THIS IS NOW THE ONLY THING IN THE DEAD-ENGINE MODEL THAT IS FITTED TO ANYTHING: the compression peak beside it is the engine's own gas load out of its displacement and compression ratio (PistonCompression.PeakNmFor), and the speed a stopped propeller breaks away at is a measurement rather than an anchor. Re-solving moves it about 0.1 because the sweep that measures the stopping speed steps 0.25 m/s. The fleet default for every type not yet solved is 3.0.
propulsion.hubXMSource: Propeller disc station, body x, m. MEASURED: docs/aircraft/extra-300-inertia-DERIVATION.md's build-up puts the MT MTV-9-B-C at +1.921 (engine +1.372, starter/alternator +1.697). The derived fallback gave +1.708 - 0.213 m too far aft, from anchoring a spinner-to-tail-post length at the rudder's trailing edge. See HubXM.
propulsion.pitchStopSource: Derived 2026-11-09 from Ty's two rules, not chosen: the FINE stop is the blade angle that lets the engine make rated rpm standing still on 26 inHg (the run-up check), and the COARSE stop is the angle needed to hold rated rpm at Vd = 1.1 x Vne (242 kt) at full power, so the governor cannot run out of blade before Vd. Power at 26 inHg is the naturally aspirated line through its friction intercept, (26-10)/(29.92-10) = 0.80 of rated. Computed by BladeElement.GovernorStops and cached here because the governor reads them every step.
propulsion.propMaterialSource: MT-Propeller MTV-9 three-blade natural-composite (wood core, glass/carbon skin)
propulsion.propInertiaSource: Propeller + spinner + the crank's rotating parts, kg.m2. DERIVED 2026-11-02 (lane/claude-inertia run 3, docs/aircraft/prop-gyro-DERIVATION.md): prop+spinner 1.95 +/- 0.15 from Hartzell's PUBLISHED polar moment for the same-class HC-C3YR (17.4 in.lb.s2 = 1.966 kg.m2, 3 composite blades on an IO-540 at 78 in), scaled to the MT MTV-9-B-C by m.D2; plus 0.14 for the AEIO-540's crank, counterweights and rod big ends. MT publishes no polar moment for the MTV-9 (EASA P.096 gives only 'approx. 24 kg'). The 2.5 this replaces was 20 % above anything the propeller and engine can have.
propulsion.coarseOnOilLossSource: Ty 2026-11-10: "aerobatic aircraft with a constant speed propeller default to high pitch with loss of oil pressure like twins do (Seminole beech 18 etc) and standard single engines default to low pitch with no oil pressure". Oil holds these blades FINE, so losing it drives them COARSE - a twin's path to feather, and on an aerobatic single what stops the prop overspeeding pointed down.

stallDynamics._separationBandNote: docs/aircraft/extra-300-airfoil-DERIVATION.md: the strip separation memory switches at each strip's OWN static stall (these tables put it near 17-21 deg) instead of the fleet's fixed 16/11 deg, whose numbers are a calibration against ~14 deg feel tables; reattachment keeps the legacy 5 deg band, which is inherited and not derived.

gear.toeOutDegSource: A standing slip angle on each main, outboard, so the pair cancel when the load is even and restore when it is not: the heavier wheel's outboard side force is the larger one, which pushes the aeroplane back toward the light side and shares the load out again. Ty 2026-11-10, flying both types: "How are the main gear tires aligned? It acts like it has toe in" - they were dead straight, which is the one thing a sprung taildragger's gear never is - then "Try 1 degree toe out both sides", and the mechanism in his own words: "The loaded tire tries to unload back to the other". 1.0 deg is his number, not a fitted one. The sign comes from the wheel's own y, so one value on both mains means outboard on both (LandingGear.ToeRad).
gear.gearTypeSource: Springy fibreglass bow -- Ty 2026-11-10: "The extra has springy fiberglass that flexes nicely." It bends rather than hinges, which is a different spring from a bungee and the same kinematics at the contact.
gear.legPivotSource: Measured off the type's own gear table and model: tools/own_models/ea300_ref_tables.json carries the composite bow as 24 measured horizontal sections, whose neutral axis runs from (span 0.418, up -0.558) where it leaves the fuselage to (span 0.790, up -1.249) at its lower end, with the axle on a bracket at span 0.890 and the tyre touching at up -1.418 (extra-300-like-own.glb, Wheels). Scaled to the config span that is a leg 0.468 m out and 0.852 m down from the root: splay 1.82. A bow has no pin -- its tip moves perpendicular to the beam as it bends, which is what a hinge at the root gives to first order -- and the root-to-contact CHORD is the conservative reading of it: Castigliano on the measured section path (integral of the moment arms about the contact, constant EI) gives 2.02 rather than 1.82, because the bow is a C whose lower half is nearly vertical.

loading._comment: seats[].eye is the seated pilot's EYE (owner Ty, approved 2026-10-31), body frame +x fwd, +y right, +z DOWN, measured on extended gear; the Cockpit camera sits exactly there. The PRIMARY seat is first. loading.seats[].station, loading.tanks[] and loading.baggage[] are the arms from docs/pending/loading-arm-estimates.md (Codex lane, 2026-11-01): a published TCDS/POH arm where the row is CONFIRMED, converted to this frame through that aircraft's anchor. maxKg is the published placard where the source gives one. referenceKg is UNCHANGED and still follows the 172's convention, so the reference loading reproduces the authored mass, CG and inertia exactly and nothing moves at spawn. Whether each airframe's authored massKg includes a pilot or fuel is still the open W&B decision in AGENT-LOG NEEDS YOU.
loading._seatPlacardNote: maxKg is a CONVENTIONAL occupant placard (250 lb, and the J-3's own authored 300 lb), not a figure read from a POH. referenceKg follows the 172's convention: the primary seat carries the pilot that mass.massKg already includes, so the reference loading still reproduces the authored mass, CG and inertia exactly and nothing moves at spawn. Whether each airframe's authored massKg really includes a pilot is the open W&B decision in AGENT-LOG NEEDS YOU.

_wingSectionNote: Wing sections extra-ma-s1..s8 (root to tip), one per strip station. Geometry and XFOIL runs derived 2026-11-02 on lane/claude-inertia run 5e; MAXIMUM LIFT SCALED TO MEASURED DATA 2026-11-10 by Ty's decision (docs/aircraft/extra-300-airfoil-DERIVATION.md sec. 1f; tools/aircraft_builder/extra_wing_table.py, method 'measured'). CANDIDATE B: the lane owner's 'ice cream cone' geometric reshape of the published Eppler E473 root / E472 tip (UIUC Airfoil Coordinates Database) at full thickness, 16.2 / 12.1 %, standing in for the unpublished MA 15 S / MA 12 S (Information Manual 1.3.3); NOT a published section. XFOIL 6.99 at each station's 1-g-stall Re, NCRIT 9, gives the shape of the curve and the post-break decline; the lift SLOPE is XFOIL x K(Re), K being Ladson's measured/XFOIL ratio for the NACA 0012 over his linear range (NASA TM 4074); and cl_max IS LADSON'S MEASURED 0012 cl_max at the station's own Reynolds number, with the break taken where the corrected curve reaches it, so the stall ANGLE follows from two measured quantities instead of from XFOIL's own peak. Ty 2026-11-10: 'scale the cl_max to the measured data ... XFOIL's optimism on the ice-cream-cone shape is not evidence.' Gault TN 3963 types every station trailing-edge, so XFOIL's own decline follows the break; each station carried to the finite wing by its own lifting-line induced angle. Run 5e's XFOIL-peak version is reproducible with --method r5e.
